source_records.abstract: Arenaviruses such as Lassa virus (LASV) and Junin virus (JUNV) can cause lethal hemorrhagic fever diseases with no FDA-approved vaccines or effective therapeutics. The arenaviral nucleoprotein (NP) contains an exoribonuclease (exoN) domain that suppresses type I interferon (IFN-I) production by degrading pathogen-associated molecular-pattern (PAMP) RNAs. The biological roles of NP exoN during viral infection have not been well characterized for highly pathogenic arenaviruses, largely due to biosafety constraints and challenges in generating viable NP exoN mutants. We previously developed a recombinant tri-segmented viral vector (rP18tri) based on non-pathogenic Pichinde virus (PICV), which allows functional studies of transgenes during arenavirus infection in a BSL-2 setting. In this study, we introduced point mutations at individual catalytic residues to abolish PICV NP exoN activity and generated exoN-deficient rP18tri(NPm) reporter viruses. These mutants failed to replicate in IFN-competent A549 cells, accompanied by strong IFN-I induction. Expression of wild-type (WT) JUNV NP, but not its exoN-deficient mutant, in the rP18tri(NPm)-G backbone restored single-cycle infectivity and suppressed IFN-I induction. Furthermore, exoN-deficient viruses produced disproportionately high levels of defective virion particles relative to virion RNA from infected A549 cells, a defect that was rescued by expression of WT JUNV NP but not the exoN-deficient NP as a transgene. Together, these data demonstrate an essential role of NP exoN in IFN-I suppression and identify a novel biological function of NP exoN in promoting the production of infectious virion particles in IFN-competent cells. In this study, we used a recombinant, tri-segmented non-pathogenic Pichinde virus (PICV) with NP exoN mutations as a safe and infectious arenavirus vector to express JUNV NP as a transgene. We found that JUNV NP exoN plays a key role in suppressing IFN-I responses and discovered a previously unrecognized function of exoN in producing infectious virion particles in IFN-competent cells. These findings improve our understanding of arenavirus infection and identify NP exoN as a promising target for developing new antiviral therapies.

title: Who leads Marburg virus research? Gender, geography and funding in authorship, 2008 to early 2023: a bibliometric baseline before the 2023-2025 outbreaks
abstract: Between 2023 and 2025, Marburg virus disease reached Equatorial Guinea, Tanzania, Rwanda and Ethiopia for the first time. WHO's 2025 Marburg research priorities make leadership of studies by local scientists a continuing goal. This study describes who led Marburg virus research before these outbreaks. I analysed 684 English-language Web of Science papers on Marburg virus published from 2008 to February 2023 (5,700 authorships). Gender was inferred from first names with Gender-API, papers about African countries were identified from their text, funders were harmonised by country and type, and themes were mapped to the WHO priorities. I used Wilson 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and logistic and negative binomial regression. Women held 35.1% (95% CI 33.9-36.4) of authorships, 41.6% (37.9-45.4) of first-author and 19.6% (16.7-22.9) of last-author positions. Women last authors rose from 15.1% (2008-2012) to 23.2% (2018-2023). Only 14.6% of papers had an author based in Africa. Of 102 papers about an African country, 25.5% (18.0-34.7) had a first author and 23.5% (16.4-32.6) a last author from that country, below benchmarks for infectious-disease research in Africa. Women based in Africa were last author on 2 papers. Of funded papers, 69.0% acknowledged a US funder (24.0% a US defence agency) and 3.2% an African funder. WHO priorities on clinical care, outbreak trials, social science and capacity strengthening each appeared in fewer than 8% of papers. An apparent citation penalty for funded papers disappeared after adjustment (rate ratio 1.07, 0.87-1.33). Before the recent outbreaks, Marburg virus research was led mostly by men in senior positions and by researchers outside the affected countries, and was funded mainly by US agencies. This baseline can track whether recent African-led responses change who leads the field.

title: Bundibugyo virus disease in outbreak settings: A practical clinical review
abstract: Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) is a severe filovirus infection caused by Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), an orthoebolavirus with diagnostic and countermeasure implications distinct from Ebola virus (EBOV). The ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has expanded substantially, with 7890 confirmed cases and 3799 deaths reported across 63 health zones in seven provinces as of 23 September 2026. BVD usually presents as a nonspecific febrile and gastrointestinal illness; haemorrhagic manifestations are uncommon at presentation. Early outbreak investigation also showed that EBOV-oriented testing can fail to detect BDBV, making species-appropriate molecular testing essential when BDBV is epidemiologically plausible. Supportive care remains the standard of management, but what can be delivered safely differs between peripheral facilities and dedicated filovirus treatment centres. First-contact facilities should prioritise recognition, separation, protected sampling, treatment of immediately life-threatening or common treatable conditions, and early referral; treatment centres can provide closer monitoring, advanced supportive care, and access to approved research protocols. Insecurity, displacement, laboratory and transport constraints, and delayed presentation continue to limit implementation. No vaccine or specific therapeutic has established clinical efficacy against BDBV in humans; Ervebo is being evaluated within research protocols and the PARTNERS trial is evaluating MBP134 and remdesivir-based regimens. This review synthesises historical and current evidence on recognition, diagnosis, clinical care, infection prevention, referral, and emerging countermeasures in outbreak-affected settings.

title: Live-cell diffracted X-ray blinking reveals Ebola virus VP40-driven budding dynamics and their regulation by cytoskeletal and lipid factors
abstract: Ebolavirus VP40 drives viral budding by remodeling the plasma membrane, yet the underlying real-time dynamics remain poorly understood. Here, we applied Diffracted X-ray Blinking (DXB) to investigate how E bolavirus VP40 affects membrane dynamics in living cells by monitoring millisecond-scale fluctuations in X-ray diffraction intensity. Expression of wild-type VP40 (wtVP40) from Zaire ebolavirus induced a progressive increase in membrane fluctuations, whereas the dimerization-defective mutant L117R and the oligomerization-deficient mutant I307R failed to enhance membrane motion despite comparable protein expression levels. Consistent with these findings, only wtVP40 was efficiently released into the culture medium, indicating that increased membrane fluctuations correlate with budding competence. DXB analysis further showed that wtVP40 increased the fast-moving population with higher decay constants, whereas the L117R and I307R mutants showed limited changes in the decay-constant distributions. Pharmacological perturbation studies demonstrated that VP40-induced membrane fluctuations are sensitive to both cytoskeletal integrity and phosphatidylserine availability. Expression of VP40 from Reston ebola virus similarly enhanced membrane dynamics, suggesting that VP40-mediated membrane remodeling is conserved among E bolaviruses . DXB-based membrane-motion analysis may therefore provide biophysical markers for viral assembly and a basis for evaluating budding-targeted antiviral strategies.

The research found that wild-type VP40 from Zaire ebolavirus significantly increased membrane motion, while dimerization and oligomerization-defective mutants did not, despite similar protein expression levels. The evidence is strong, with clear results and implications for understanding viral mechanisms.

abstract_zh: 埃博拉病毒VP40通过重塑细胞膜驱动病毒出芽,但其背后的实时动态机制仍不明确。在这里,我们应用了散射X射线闪烁(DXB)技术,通过监测毫秒级尺度的X射线衍射强度波动,研究VP40如何影响活细胞中的膜动态。来自扎伊尔埃博拉病毒的野生型VP40(wtVP40)表达导致膜波动逐渐增加,而二聚化缺陷型突变体L117R和寡聚化缺陷型突变体I307R尽管蛋白表达水平相当,却未能增强膜运动。这些结果一致表明,只有wtVP40能有效释放到培养基中,说明膜波动的增加与出芽能力相关。DXB分析进一步显示,wtVP40增加了具有较高衰减常数的快速运动群体,而L117R和I307R突变体在衰减常数分布上变化有限。药理学扰动研究表明,VP40诱导的膜波动对细胞骨架完整性和磷脂酰丝氨酸的可用性均敏感。来自雷斯顿埃博拉病毒的VP40表达同样增强了膜动态,表明VP40介导的膜重塑在埃博拉病毒中是保守的。因此,基于DXB的膜运动分析可能为病毒组装提供生物物理标志,并为针对出芽的策略评估奠定基础。

title: Beyond isolation: Clinical care as an outbreak control intervention for Ebola disease

full_text: Outbreak control and clinical care are often treated as separate domains. Clinical teams care for patients after admission, whereas public health teams detect cases, conduct contact tracing, organize isolation, communicate risk, and prevent unsafe burials. This separation may be administratively convenient, but it is epidemiologically misleading. In cases of Ebola, care quality and accessibility can influence whether patients disclose symptoms, when they enter isolation, and where they spend the most infectious phase of illness, as well as whether communities cooperate with response actions. Therefore, clinical care is not merely the humanitarian endpoint of an Ebola response. It is an active intervention for outbreak control. The 2026 Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda unfolded amid insecurity, population movement, restricted healthcare access, and pressure on treatment services. With no licensed Bundibugyo virus-specific vaccine or treatment, early recognition, safe referral, infection prevention, and structured supportive care are central to the response.[] The success of isolation, surveillance, and community engagement partly depends on whether the clinical system offers patients a credible chance of recovery. Care determines when isolation begins Ebola transmission frequently occurs before patients reach specialized treatment facilities. Early symptoms are nonspecific and may be mistaken for malaria, enteric infection, or other common febrile illnesses. Patients may remain at home, consult traditional healers, attend private clinics, or move between general healthcare facilities. As the illness progresses, physical caregiving intensifies, and exposure to infectious body fluids increases. The interval between symptom onset and protected care thus represents a clinical delay and is a period within which household, community, and healthcare-associated transmission potentially occurs. Communities do not decide whether to report an illness solely based on public health messages encouraging symptom reporting and early care seeking; they also judge what is likely to happen after reporting. Studies conducted in Sierra Leone have found that during the 2014–2016 West African Ebola epidemic, trust in Ebola treatment centers was shaped by experiences of care, communication, survival, and institutional behavior.[] Clinical quality shapes transmission not by altering viral biology but by changing the timing and location of infectious contact. Accessible, trustworthy care can encourage earlier presentation, allowing patients to spend a greater proportion of their infectious period in settings designed for isolation and infection prevention rather than in unprotected households or ordinary clinics. Treatment centers must be places of care An isolation space is not necessarily a treatment bed. Functional Ebola care requires trained staff, continuous nursing observation, essential medicines, basic laboratory support, reliable supplies, infection prevention, water, electricity, and safe waste management. Supportive care includes assessing and treating dehydration, electrolyte and glucose abnormalities, shock, hypoxemia, pain, distress, and coinfections and addressing the specific needs of children and pregnant women.[] Early admission is important. An analysis of patients treated during the 2018–2020 Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo showed that each additional day between symptom onset and treatment center admission was associated with increased mortality, although those patients had Ebola virus disease and access to effective monoclonal antibodies.[] This finding cannot be extended directly to Bundibugyo virus disease, but the underlying principle is relevant: Delayed entry into care can allow further clinical deterioration and prolong opportunities for unprotected exposure. Clinical quality is not the sole determinant of survival. Outcomes depend on the viral species, viral load, and disease severity as well as the patient’s age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, and access to specific treatment. A center that offers little beyond separation may reinforce the belief that admission has no benefit. A center that provides competent, compassionate care can produce visible survivors and make early referrals more acceptable. Isolation removes infectious patients from a community; quality treatment gives the community a reason to accept that removal. Trust is reinforced or undermined at the bedside Community engagement is primarily seen as communication oriented—that is, explaining transmission, addressing rumors, encouraging reporting, and promoting safe burial. These activities are indispensable, but communication cannot compensate indefinitely for poor clinical experience. Trust is produced not only by what response teams say but also by what patients and families observe them doing: whether suffering is treated, information is shared, families are allowed to maintain safe contact, and patients are treated with dignity. During the 2018–2019 outbreak in North Kivu, low institutional trust and belief in misinformation were associated with lower acceptance of preventive behaviors and vaccination.[] This does not mean that better care alone creates trust. Political history, insecurity, inequality, coercive practices, and local customs remain important influences. A damaging feedback loop can emerge when limited or inaccessible care leads to delayed presentation, advanced disease, high observed mortality, and an increased fear of treatment centers. The reverse is also plausible: Accessible, effective, and dignified care can lead to visible recovery, which may strengthen trust, encourage earlier presentation, and reduce unprotected exposure (Figure 1). Thus, community trust is partly a clinical outcome. The Ebola care system extends beyond treatment centers Patients with unrecognized Ebola disease often first attend community clinics, emergency departments, maternity services, private hospitals, pharmacies, or facilities treating presumed malaria or bacterial infections. Early experiences from the 2026 Bundibugyo virus outbreak highlight healthcare worker infections, unsafe triage approaches, limited isolation capacity, and infection prevention vulnerabilities.[] Therefore, ordinary facilities must be able to recognize compatible syndromes, obtain exposure histories, initiate precautions, safely isolate patients with suspected Ebola disease, provide initial stabilization, notify public health authorities, and arrange protected transfers. These capabilities must coexist with continued care for common febrile illnesses, as most patients presenting with fever will not have Ebola disease. During the 2014–2015 outbreak in Tonkolili District, Sierra Leone, the opening of an Ebola management center closer to the affected communities was associated with a reduction in median symptom-to-admission time from six to three days.[] A larger retrospective study of the 2018–2020 outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo found that patients presenting to decentralized facilities integrated into existing healthcare structures had modestly shorter admission delays than those presenting to centralized facilities.[] The objective is not universal decentralization but a tiered care network that reduces the geographic, social, and institutional distance between symptom onset and effective treatment. This network would comprise frontline facilities able to recognize, temporarily isolate, and stabilize suspected cases; decentralized units that provide protected assessment and care closer to affected communities; and referral centers that have the capacity for patients requiring more intensive support. Proximity should thus be treated as a clinical and epidemiologic design variable rather than a mere logistical consideration. From principle to practice Translating this principle into practice requires several changes in outbreak preparedness and response. First, the rapid expansion of isolation capacity should be accompanied by a minimum clinical care package with sufficient numbers of appropriately trained staff, continuous nursing care, basic supportive treatment, infection prevention, essential diagnostics, and reliable supplies. Preparedness assessments should measure functional treatment capacity rather than designated bed numbers alone. Second, quality-of-care indicators should be incorporated into outbreak monitoring alongside case detection, laboratory turnaround, and contact follow-up. The time from symptom onset to protected care and the proportion of designated beds capable of delivering continuous, staffed, and supplied care are examples of measures that closely reflect operational readiness. Third, the WHO, ministries of health, and response partners should establish tiered referral networks that link frontline facilities, decentralized care units, and higher-level treatment centers before case numbers surge. Evidence on proximity suggests that bringing protected care closer to affected communities can shorten admission delays.[] Emphasizing quality does not mean delaying the urgently needed expansion of isolation capacity. During rapid epidemic growth, additional physical space may be required before ideal staffing or infrastructure is available. However, physical capacity and functional capacity should not be considered equivalent. Expansion should proceed with a minimum threshold of staffing, infection prevention, basic supportive care, and supply continuity before a bed is counted toward operational treatment capacity. Additional capabilities can then be introduced as resources permit. The relevant trade-off is not simply capacity versus quality but how rapidly physical isolation capacity can be converted into safe and functional clinical capacity. Clinical care is an upstream intervention Governments, health systems, and response partners have an ethical obligation to provide clinical care to patients affected by Ebola outbreaks. This obligation alone justifies investment in care; the additional epidemiological value of that investment should also be recognized. Investment by these actors in nursing, supportive care, infection prevention, referrals, family communication, and the preparedness of ordinary hospitals may improve survival and reduce suffering. It may also make early reporting more acceptable, reduce household caregiving during advanced illness stages, prevent healthcare-associated amplification, and decrease deaths outside protected settings. Contemporary proposals to embed Ebola treatment within stronger health systems emphasize access, dignity, safety, and integration with routine services.[] Clinical teams do not operate downstream of outbreak control. They help determine whether surveillance alerts become patients in care, whether isolation is accepted, and whether community engagement is reinforced or contradicted by lived experiences. Ebola strategies should therefore present treatment centers as places where patients receive the best achievable chance of recovery, not merely as places where infection is contained. Quality clinical care during Ebola outbreaks is not a measure taken after transmission control succeeds. Rather, it is one of the conditions that makes transmission control possible. Funding None. Treatment centers must be places of care An isolation space is not necessarily a treatment bed. Functional Ebola care requires trained staff, continuous nursing observation, essential medicines, basic laboratory support, reliable supplies, infection prevention, water, electricity, and safe waste management. Supportive care includes assessing and treating dehydration, electrolyte and glucose abnormalities, shock, hypoxemia, pain, distress, and coinfections and addressing the specific needs of children and pregnant women.[] Early admission is important. An analysis of patients treated during the 2018–2020 Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo showed that each additional day between symptom onset and treatment center admission was associated with increased mortality, although those patients had Ebola virus disease and access to effective monoclonal antibodies.[] This finding cannot be extended directly to Bundibugyo virus disease, but the underlying principle is relevant: Delayed entry into care can allow further clinical deterioration and prolong opportunities for unprotected exposure. Clinical quality is not the sole determinant of survival. Outcomes depend on the viral species, viral load, and disease severity as well as the patient’s age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, and access to specific treatment. A center that offers little beyond separation may reinforce the belief that admission has no benefit. A center that provides competent, compassionate care can produce visible survivors and make early referrals more acceptable. Isolation removes infectious patients from a community; quality treatment gives the community a reason to accept that removal. Trust is produced not only by what response teams say but also by what patients and families observe them doing: whether suffering is treated, information is shared, families are allowed to maintain safe contact, and patients are treated with dignity. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to challenge the conventional separation of outbreak control and clinical care in Ebola disease, highlighting the need to recognize clinical care as an integral part of outbreak management. Limitations include the lack of direct experimental evidence and potential biases in community behavior reporting.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在挑战埃博拉病毒病中暴发控制与临床护理的传统分离,强调应将临床护理视为暴发管理的重要组成部分。背景强调,这种分离在行政上可能方便,但在流行病学上是误导性的。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究分析了2026年刚果民主共和国和乌干达由邦迪布古病毒引起的埃博拉暴发,重点探讨了临床护理在暴发动态中的作用。研究考虑了患者可能采取的多样化路径,包括家庭、传统治疗师、私人诊所和一般医疗机构。
elements_zh.methods: 研究方法涉及考察2026年暴发期间临床护理质量、患者行为与传播动态之间的相互作用。包括回顾护理经验、沟通、生存率以及机构行为,这些因素塑造了患者对治疗中心的信任。
elements_zh.main_results: 研究结果表明,患者对埃博拉治疗中心的信任受到护理质量、沟通、生存率和机构行为的影响。发现临床护理质量通过改变传染接触的时间和地点,影响了传播的动态。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为临床护理不仅是人道主义终点,而且是暴发控制的主动干预措施。这一见解在将临床护理作为暴发应对策略关键组成部分的框架上具有新颖性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现强调了将临床护理整合到暴发控制工作中的重要性,突出了建立可及且值得信赖的治疗设施的必要性,以鼓励患者早期就诊并降低传播风险。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的局限性在于其依赖观察性数据,且缺乏直接的实验证据。然而,由于其关注真实世界暴发动态和社区行为,证据强度中等。

abstract_zh: 对2018–2020年刚果民主共和国埃博拉暴发期间接受治疗的患者进行分析显示,症状出现与治疗中心入院之间每增加一天,都会与死亡率增加相关,尽管这些患者接受了埃博拉病毒病治疗并获得了有效的单克隆抗体。[] 这一发现不能直接推广到邦迪布古病毒病,但其基本原理是相关的:延迟进入护理可能会导致进一步的临床恶化,并延长无保护暴露的机会。在2014–2015年塞拉利昂通科利里区的埃博拉暴发期间,开设一个更接近受影响社区的埃博拉管理中心,使中位症状到入院时间从6天减少到3天。[] 对2018–2020年刚果民主共和国埃博拉暴发的更大规模回顾性研究发现,前往分散式设施(这些设施整合到现有卫生体系中)的患者,其入院延迟时间比前往集中式设施的患者略短。[] 目标并非是普遍的分散化,而是建立一个分级护理网络,以减少症状出现与有效治疗之间的地理、社会和制度距离。通常将暴发控制与临床护理视为两个独立领域。临床团队负责患者入院后的护理,而公共卫生团队则负责病例检测、接触追踪、组织隔离、风险沟通和防止不安全葬礼。这种分离在行政上可能方便,但在流行病学上是误导性的。在埃博拉病例中,护理质量与可及性可能影响患者是否披露症状、何时进入隔离以及在最传染性阶段在哪里度过。

full_text: I visited a family of 19 in Sierra Leone in 2015. By the time I arrived, eight had died. The other 11 were left to live with the grief and fear of what might happen next. I am a medical doctor and epidemiologist, and at that time I was serving on an African Union Ebola response mission. The 2014-16 epidemic in West Africa caused more than 28,600 cases and 11,300 deaths. Over roughly six months in Sierra Leone, I saw how quickly the disease could overwhelm families and health services. That’s also when I learned that good medical advice can fail if people do not trust those delivering it. Some families buried relatives secretly, despite warnings. In certain communities, funeral practices included washing the body and sprinkling water on mourners, which risked exposing people to infected bodily fluids. Simply repeating instructions did not help. But those of us working in the field found that working with families to make burials safer while respecting their grief helped them to mourn their loss while stopping the virus from spreading. More than a decade later, those experiences have returned to my mind. The Ebola outbreak now sweeping across parts of Central Africa is different from the one I responded to. Still, one lesson remains: Timely international support makes a huge difference. A growing outbreak The current outbreak was declared in the Democratic Republic of Congo, or DRC, in May 2026. By Oct. 28, 2026, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 10,305 confirmed cases and 4,996 deaths across five countries, with new updates daily. The DRC accounts for nearly all of those cases and deaths. This is already the second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded, after the 2014-16 epidemic. The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, whereas the 2014-16 epidemic involved a different Ebola virus. No vaccine or specific treatment is currently approved for Bundibugyo. The World Health Organization warns that late detection, deaths outside health facilities and sustained transmission in the DRC remain serious concerns. The DRC has extensive experience with responding to outbreaks, and African institutions are coordinating a continental response. Africa has the expertise and leadership. What it needs right now is sustained support that reaches the front line – quickly, safely and accountably. Crossing borders Ebola follows human movement. In October, Kenya reported infections linked to a traveler who had passed through Uganda from the DRC. Nigeria also reported an imported case around the same time. Symptoms can appear between two and 21 days after exposure, and people are generally not infectious before symptoms begin. A traveler may therefore pass a temperature check and become ill days later. These events show why countries need to share information quickly, verify travel histories and maintain contact tracing across borders. What international support looks like now International partners are, in fact, contributing. In September 2026, the United States reported US$887 million in Ebola-related health and humanitarian assistance. The U.K. announced a contribution of roughly £78 million ($104 million). In October, the World Bank described $426.6 million in current and planned financing for the DRC and neighboring countries. And Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention reported nearly $3 billion in international pledges following a September mobilization effort. But pledges are not the same as supplies delivered or services provided, and these contributions are coming late in the outbreak. In 2014, Britain helped expand treatment and safe-burial operations in Sierra Leone. The U.S. mobilized logistics capacity in Liberia, while France assisted Guinea. And African Union health workers served alongside local teams and other partners. That cooperation saved lives, though the global response was slow to scale up. It has been discouraging for me to see that today’s response has not built on that experience without waiting for the outbreak to grow further. According to the WHO, massive cuts to international aid over the past year diminished a quicker response. The success of international collaboration will be measured in how many contacts are reached, how rapidly patients are tested, how many health workers have protective equipment and are consistently paid, whether women can still deliver babies safely, and whether remote communities can get care. Building connections with everyday people My experience in Sierra Leone in 2014 taught me that trust is essential to outbreak control. Families need credible explanations, timely information and opportunities to ask questions. Local health workers, faith leaders, survivors and community organizations can help bridge the gap between an emergency response and the people it seeks to protect. That gap can be large even when a disease is widely known. A colleague and I conducted a study involving 440 secondary school students in Nigeria in 2014, and we found that 95.4% had heard of Ebola. Yet only 42.3% identified fever as a possible symptom, and only 33.2% recognized the risk associated with certain burial practices. Seeing that awareness of the disease alone was not enough, we subsequently began Ebola education activities in local Nigerian schools. The need for reliable information from trusted sources remains in 2026. Risk messages must be consistent, culturally sensitive and practical. This works only when communities are partners in recognizing illness, seeking early care, contact follow-up and safe, dignified burials. Even in times of emergency, health workers cannot treat communities simply as audiences for instructions. Reaching affected communities In August 2026, Africa CDC and the WHO jointly called for expanded laboratory and treatment capacity and faster delivery of supplies. But in the DRC, insecurity and displacement due to ongoing conflict, in addition to poor roads, can prevent supplies and patients from reaching treatment centers. These obstacles may also keep laboratories from receiving samples and contact-tracing teams from visiting households. The ministry of health is not equipped to resolve these problems. The response therefore requires cooperation among health authorities, humanitarian agencies, local government, transport services and those responsible for civilian safety. There are signs that investments in these services are helping. In October, the World Bank reported that supported detection timelines in the DRC had improved. This meant new cases were being detected within one or two days by September, a huge improvement from the 10-day detection timeline early in the outbreak. Looking to the future Because Bundibugyo virus lacks an approved vaccine or specific treatment, this outbreak also demands carefully conducted research. The Tumaini vaccine trial, begun in Bunia, DRC, in October 2026, is an important step toward a potential vaccine. The hope is that this effort will prevent more families from experiencing loss. I still remember the 11 survivors in that Sierra Leone household I visited back in 2015. I never learned what ultimately happened to them, but more than a decade later, I still think about them.

source_body_en: A colleague and I conducted a study involving 440 secondary school students in Nigeria in 2014, and we found that 95.4% had heard of Ebola. I visited a family of 19 in Sierra Leone in 2015. By the time I arrived, eight had died. The other 11 were left to live with the grief and fear of what might happen next. I am a medical doctor and epidemiologist, and at that time I was serving on an African Union Ebola response mission. The 2014-16 epidemic in West Africa caused more than 28,600 cases and 11,300 deaths. Over roughly six months in Sierra Leone, I saw how quickly the disease could overwhelm families and health services. That’s also when I learned that good medical advice can fail if people do not trust those delivering it. Some families buried relatives secretly, despite warnings. In certain communities, funeral practices included washing the body and sprinkling water on mourners, which risked exposing people to infected bodily fluids. Simply repeating instructions did not help. But those of us working in the field found that working with families to make burials safer while respecting their grief helped them to mourn their loss while stopping the virus from spreading. More than a decade later, those experiences have returned to my mind. The Ebola outbreak now sweeping across parts of Central Africa is different from the one I responded to. Still, one lesson remains: Timely international support makes a huge difference. A growing outbreak The current outbreak was declared in the Democratic Republic of Congo, or DRC, in May 2026. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 10,305 confirmed cases and 4,996 deaths across five countries, with new updates daily. The DRC accounts for nearly all of those cases and deaths. Arts + Culture Economy Education Environment + Energy Ethics + Religion Health Politics + Society Science + Tech World Podcasts Local The DRC is in the seventh month of an Ebola outbreak. AP Photo/Sebastien Kitsa Musayi Delayed international support has hampered efforts to contain and treat Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo Published: November 5, 2026 8:36am EST I visited a family of 19 in Sierra Leone in 2015. By the time I arrived, eight had died. The other 11 were left to live with the grief and fear of what might happen next. I am a medical doctor and epidemiologist, and at that time I was serving on an African Union Ebola response mission. The 2014-16 epidemic in West Africa caused more than 28,600 cases and 11,300 deaths. Over roughly six months in Sierra Leone, I saw how quickly the disease could overwhelm families and health services. That’s also when I learned that good medical advice can fail if people do not trust those delivering it. Some families buried relatives secretly, despite warnings. In certain communities, funeral practices included washing the body and sprinkling water on mourners, which risked exposing people to infected bodily fluids. Simply repeating instructions did not help. But those of us working in the field found that working with families to make burials safer while respecting their grief helped them to mourn their loss while stopping the virus from spreading. More than a decade later, those experiences have returned to my mind. The Ebola outbreak now sweeping across parts of Central Africa is different from the one I responded to. Still, one lesson remains: Timely international support makes a huge difference. A growing outbreak The current outbreak was declared in the Democratic Republic of Congo, or DRC, in May 2026. By Oct. 28, 2026, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 10,305 confirmed cases and 4,996 deaths across five countries, with new updates daily. The DRC accounts for nearly all of those cases and deaths. This is already the second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded, after the 2014-16 epidemic. The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, whereas the 2014-16 epidemic involved a different Ebola virus. No vaccine or specific treatment is currently approved for Bundibugyo. The World Health Organization warns that late detection, deaths outside health facilities and sustained transmission in the DRC remain serious concerns. The DRC has extensive experience with responding to outbreaks, and African institutions are coordinating a continental response. Africa has the expertise and leadership. What it needs right now is sustained support that reaches the front line – quickly, safely and accountably. Crossing borders Ebola follows human movement. In October, Kenya reported infections linked to a traveler who had passed through Uganda from the DRC. Nigeria also reported an imported case around the same time. Symptoms can appear between two and 21 days after exposure, and people are generally not infectious before symptoms begin. A traveler may therefore pass a temperature check and become ill days later. These events show why countries need to share information quickly, verify travel histories and maintain contact tracing across borders. In response to the 2014 Ebola outbreak, American healthcare workers set up makeshift clinics like this one outside Monrovia, Liberia. Abbas Dulleh/AP What international support looks like now International partners are, in fact, contributing. In September 2026, the United States reported US$887 million in Ebola-related health and humanitarian assistance. The U.K. announced a contribution of roughly £78 million ($104 million). In October, the World Bank described $426.6 million in current and planned financing for the DRC and neighboring countries. And Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention reported nearly $3 billion in international pledges following a September mobilization effort. But pledges are not the same as supplies delivered or services provided, and these contributions are coming late in the outbreak. In 2014, Britain helped expand treatment and safe-burial operations in Sierra Leone. The U.S. mobilized logistics capacity in Liberia, while France assisted Guinea. And African Union health workers served alongside local teams and other partners. That cooperation saved lives, though the global response was slow to scale up. It has been discouraging for me to see that today’s response has not built on that experience without waiting for the outbreak to grow further. According to the WHO, massive cuts to international aid over the past year diminished a quicker response. The success of international collaboration will be measured in how many contacts are reached, how rapidly patients are tested, how many health workers have protective equipment and are consistently paid, whether women can still deliver babies safely, and whether remote communities can get care. Building connections with everyday people My experience in Sierra Leone in 2014 taught me that trust is essential to outbreak control. Families need credible explanations, timely information and opportunities to ask questions. Local health workers, faith leaders, survivors and community organizations can help bridge the gap between an emergency response and the people it seeks to protect. That gap can be large even when a disease is widely known. A colleague and I conducted a study involving 440 secondary school students in Nigeria in 2014, and we found that 95.4% had heard of Ebola. Yet only 42.3% identified fever as a possible symptom, and only 33.2% recognized the risk associated with certain burial practices. Seeing that awareness of the disease alone was not enough, we subsequently began Ebola education activities in local Nigerian schools. The need for reliable information from trusted sources remains in 2026. Risk messages must be consistent, culturally sensitive and practical. This works only when communities are partners in recognizing illness, seeking early care, contact follow-up and safe, dignified burials. Even in times of emergency, health workers cannot treat communities simply as audiences for instructions. Reaching affected communities In August 2026, Africa CDC and the WHO jointly called for expanded laboratory and treatment capacity and faster delivery of supplies. But in the DRC, insecurity and displacement due to ongoing conflict, in addition to poor roads, can prevent supplies and patients from reaching treatment centers. These obstacles may also keep laboratories from receiving samples and contact-tracing teams from visiting households. The ministry of health is not equipped to resolve these problems. The response therefore requires cooperation among health authorities, humanitarian agencies, local government, transport services and those responsible for civilian safety. There are signs that investments in these services are helping. In October, the World Bank reported that supported detection timelines in the DRC had improved. This meant new cases were being detected within one or two days by September, a huge improvement from the 10-day detection timeline early in the outbreak. The Tumaini vaccine trials started in the DRC at the end of October 2026. ‘Tumaini’ is the Swahili word for hope. AP Photo/Dieudonne Dirole Looking to the future Because Bundibugyo virus lacks an approved vaccine or specific treatment, this outbreak also demands carefully conducted research. The Tumaini vaccine trial, begun in Bunia, DRC, in October 2026, is an important step toward a potential vaccine. The hope is that this effort will prevent more families from experiencing loss. I still remember the 11 survivors in that Sierra Leone household I visited back in 2015. I never learned what ultimately happened to them, but more than a decade later, I still think about them.
